lesson.title: Valid but untrue

steps.headline: An argument is valid when no case has all its premises true and its conclusion false.

lead.text: Validity asks about the link between premises and conclusion. It doesn't ask whether the premises are true. In the hook, if the premises held, Ana would have to be rich.
Test “p → q; p; therefore q” against the four rows. You are looking for a row where both premises are true and q is false.

reveal.text: Compare your answer with the rows. Wherever p → q and p are both true, q is true as well.

steps.headline: A counterexample is a case that makes every premise true and the conclusion false.

lead.text: It is the one thing a valid argument cannot have. Valid means no such case exists.

steps.headline: Is “p ∨ q; q; therefore p” valid?

workedSteps.text: Look for a row where both premises are true.
In FT, p ∨ q and q are true, but the conclusion p is false.
A counterexample exists, so the argument is not valid.

lead.text: Look for a counterexample in this argument. Set p false and q true.

steps.headline: A valid argument whose premises are all true is sound.

lead.text: Soundness needs both parts. Validity checks the link. Evidence checks the premises, one by one.
A false conclusion tempts people to blame the reasoning. Test the link first.

lesson.orientation: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.
lesson.nextAction: Recognise that a conclusion can follow from false premises.

blocks.text: “Everyone who owns a dragon is rich. Ana owns a dragon. So Ana is rich.” There are no dragons.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge validity from the cases alone, and say when a valid argument is still unsound.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no case makes the premises true and the conclusion false. It is sound only if it is valid and its premises are true.

blocks.text: You saw that the dragon argument follows even though its first premise is false. You found a counterexample to “p → q; q; therefore p”, with p false and q true.

recap.nextHook: Some invalid patterns look valid. Name the most common ones.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Ask whether both premises can be true while q is false.
The first premise links p to q, and the second states p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No row makes both premises true and q false.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. In every row where both premises hold, q holds too.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: How many counterexamples may a valid argument have?
hints: Validity says no case has true premises and a false conclusion.
What does the definition allow for such cases?
Count the exceptions it permits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A single counterexample would make it invalid, so a valid argument has none.

questions.onCorrect: None. One counterexample would make the argument invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: One counterexample is enough to make an argument invalid. How many does validity permit?
Validity is a guarantee over every case. How many exceptions does that allow?

questions.prompt: Is the argument “p → q; q; therefore p” valid or invalid?
hints: Try p false and q true in the argument.
Check both premises, then compare them with the conclusion p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The false–true row is a counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. With p false and q true, both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the row with p false and q true. Do both premises hold, and what happens to p?

questions.prompt: A valid argument contains a false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Soundness needs two things: validity and true premises.
Does the stated premise meet the second?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires validity and all true premises.

questions.onCorrect: Unsound. Soundness needs every premise to be true as well as validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity alone isn't enough. What does soundness also ask of the premises?

questions.prompt: A valid argument has all true premises. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Recall both parts of the definition of soundness.
The question gives you validity and true premises.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It meets both requirements for soundness.

questions.onCorrect: Sound. It is valid and every premise is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Soundness needs validity and true premises. Does this argument have both?

questions.prompt: How many true-premise, false-conclusion cases are needed to refute validity?
hints: Validity says there are no cases with true premises and a false conclusion.
One exception breaks a promise about every case.
You don't need most of the table to be counterexamples.
questions.onCorrect: One. A single case with true premises and a false conclusion refutes validity.

misconceptions.feedback: With no such case, the argument is valid. How many are needed to refute it?
You don't need several. Validity promises there are none.

questions.prompt: If the first two sentences were true, would Ana have to be rich? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the first two sentences are true. What follows about Ana?
Ignore whether dragons exist.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A dragon owner is rich, and Ana owns one.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. If the premises held, Ana would have to be rich. Whether they hold is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Suppose the first two sentences are true, whatever the real world is like. Could Ana avoid being rich?

questions.prompt: All the premises of a valid argument are true. Must its conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Is there any case with true premises and a false conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion. What does that leave?

questions.prompt: Why is one counterexample enough to show an argument invalid?
hints: What does validity promise about cases?

acceptedIdeas: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validity promises no case with true premises and a false conclusion. One is enough to break it.

questions.onCorrect: Validity is a promise about every case, so a single exception breaks it.

choices.label: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
Most of the rows have to be counterexamples.
The premises are false in all the other rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity allows no such case at all. It is not a matter of how many.
The other rows don't matter. Validity is about cases with true premises.

questions.prompt: “All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.” A learner says: “It's invalid, because the conclusion is false.” Is the learner right? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the premises are true. Could the conclusion still be false?
Is a false conclusion the same as an invalid argument?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. The argument is valid but unsound.

questions.onCorrect: No. The conclusion follows from the premises, so it is valid. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: A false conclusion doesn't make an argument invalid. Ask whether true premises would force it.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Find the rows where both premises are true.
Is q true in every one of them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the row with p false and q true keeps both premises true, and q is true there.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. The only row where both premises hold is FT, and q is true there.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p ∨ q and ¬p are both true and q is false. Is there one?
